latinFallbacksInT.fallback: Punic stelae, Roman Africa proconsularis, and the Byrsa hill remain the oldest onomastic layer of Tunisian genealogy — names, places, and Mediterranean crossings that still echo in family memory.

The Aghlabid and Fatimid capital preserved nasab chains, waqf deeds, and jurisprudential manuscripts. Kairouan remains a primary key for tracing scholarly and tribal lineages across the Sahel and the interior.

Charaïque court registers, beylical decrees, and majba tax rolls document marriages, inheritances, and habous from Tunis, Sfax, and the medinas. These sijillat are the backbone of pre-colonial pedigree work.
État civil from 1886 onward, Protectorate cadastre, and republican identity papers connect living families to the older documentary chain — 24 governorates, one indexed research surface.
About Roots Tunisia — Carthage to the civil registry
Roots Tunisia preserves Tunisian lineage through Carthage, Kairouan, Ottoman sijillat, civil registry, and the 24 governorates.
A Tunisian archive of names, places, and periods
From Punic Carthage and Fatimid Kairouan to Ottoman sijillat and modern état civil, Roots Tunisia holds family evidence across twenty-four governorates.
Why Tunisian genealogy needs its own house

Tunisian families are documented in more than one script, court, and language. A pedigree may begin with a CIN extract in Sousse, pass through a Tunis qadi sijill, and rest on a habous deed in Kairouan. Roots Tunisia keeps those layers together.
Nasab, waqf, and the Great Mosque
Kairouan’s manuscript culture and pious endowments are not decoration. They are how families recorded descent, property, and scholarship from the Aghlabids through the Hafsids.
Sijillat from charaïque courts, beylical chancery, and majba rolls name spouses, witnesses, neighbourhoods, and estates. They sit beside Protectorate état civil rather than beneath it.

Privacy policy and data protection guidelines for Roots Tunisia researchers and families.
Roots Tunisia respects the sensitivity of family heritage and genealogical records. We are committed to protecting the privacy of living individuals and securing archival data.

Details concerning living persons (born less than 100 years ago without death records) are automatically privatized by default and hidden from public searches unless explicitly shared by the tree owner.
We collect account details (name, email, governorate/region), user-uploaded GEDCOM files, oral history recordings, and research inquiries submitted to our team.
All genealogical databases and document stores are encrypted in transit and at rest, adhering to Tunisian data protection regulations and modern cybersecurity standards.
Clear, fair, and transparent billing terms for our Tunisian and international researchers.

Roots Tunisia is dedicated to transparent, honest pricing. We do not use hidden fees, deceptive cancellation barriers, or unexpected recurring add-ons. You can manage or cancel your subscription at any time.
You may cancel your recurring monthly or annual plan at any time through your User Settings dashboard or by emailing our team at
Upon cancellation, your subscription access will continue uninterrupted until the end of your current paid billing period. You will not be billed again.

In compliance with international and European consumer protection standards, customers in applicable jurisdictions (including the EU and UK) have the right to withdraw from their initial subscription purchase within 14 calendar days of transaction date for a full refund.
If you activated immediate digital delivery and conducted extensive bulk archival downloads during this window, refunds may be adjusted to account for the service utilized prior to withdrawal.

Due to the immediate access nature of high-resolution digital scans, historical certificates, and GEDCOM tree files, one-time document processing fees are non-refundable once the file has been successfully delivered or downloaded, except in cases where:
The downloaded file is corrupted, illegible, or unreadable due to technical server defects.
The wrong archival record was delivered due to our administrative error.
